content: To identify the geographical areas and demographic groups (by age, sex, and population type) with the highest burden of undiagnosed hepatitis B or C infections, it is necessary to analyze all available epidemiological data. This includes data from surveillance systems, surveys, and healthcare programs. While it is challenging to determine the exact number of individuals with chronic hepatitis B or C or the number of new infections in a specific area, estimates can be derived from these data sources. Population-based household surveys often fail to reach or identify high-risk populations and marginalized groups. Therefore, additional studies targeting these groups may be required. For example, estimates of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody prevalence should be stratified by location, age group, and specific high-risk populations. This includes data from national household surveys and surveillance data, such as those collected from pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) clinics. For high-risk groups with elevated prevalence rates, it is essential to determine the prevalence of chronic infection within these groups, estimate the proportion of the infected population belonging to these groups, and calculate the size of these populations. Once prevalence data for the general population and specific groups are summarized, this information can guide the selection of target groups for testing services. Testing high-prevalence groups may yield higher positivity rates but may identify a smaller proportion of the total infected population. Conversely, testing the general population or specific age or birth cohorts may yield lower positivity rates but identify a larger proportion of infected individuals. Hepatitis testing uptake should be monitored across different populations and testing approaches. This includes tracking the proportion of individuals tested who are positive, stratified by population, testing method, or facility. Additionally, the number and proportion of individuals aware of their hepatitis B or C status should be assessed. This may include those who have ever been tested or those tested within the past 12 months and received their results. These data should be disaggregated by sex, age, geographical region, population type, testing approach, and facility. The proportion of individuals who test positive and are subsequently enrolled in hepatitis care and treatment services should also be evaluated. Testing and treatment coverage targets should be established for each type of testing service. These targets may include the number of individuals to be tested and referred for care and treatment or prevention services if they are uninfected but at high ongoing risk. An additional target may involve the proportion of individuals living with viral hepatitis who are diagnosed. Consolidating these targets across all services will result in an overall goal for testing and treatment. Testing and treatment targets must be directly linked, as the primary purpose of diagnosing chronic hepatitis B and C is to enable access to treatment. Plans for scaling up treatment services will fail without adequate testing, and large-scale testing efforts will have limited impact without concurrent expansion of treatment capacity. Following an epidemiological analysis, a detailed assessment and mapping of current hepatitis testing activities and coverage should be conducted. This includes identifying the locations of all testing settings and sites, uptake and coverage rates (by sex, age, and population), and funding sources. Testing services may include facility-based testing in ANC, tuberculosis (TB), and sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics, harm reduction programs, outpatient and inpatient services, community-based and mobile testing, workplace or educational institution testing, and private healthcare providers. A situational assessment of HIV testing services should also be undertaken, as the same populations may be affected, providing opportunities to integrate hepatitis testing into existing HIV testing models. The assessment should include an inventory of resources needed and available for testing services, such as testing kits, financial resources, and human resources. Financial resources for hepatitis testing, including government investments and funding from partners, should also be evaluated. The costs and cost-effectiveness of different testing approaches should be assessed. Cost comparisons between countries can be challenging due to variations in healthcare systems, personnel costs, and population accessibility. Direct cost comparisons are more interpretable when standardized inputs are used. Cost-effectiveness analyses compare the costs and health impacts of different interventions to identify those providing the best value for money. Health outcomes used in these analyses include the number of people tested, hepatitis B or C cases identified, infections averted (e.g., through vaccination or prevention of mother-to-child transmission), and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained. The health benefits of testing are derived from subsequent treatment and prevention interventions, emphasizing the importance of effective linkage from testing to treatment. Program costs and cost-effectiveness depend on the specifics of the program design. For example, mobile testing camps targeting people who inject drugs (PWID) may have significantly different costs compared to fixed-location testing in drug treatment programs. Both approaches may be necessary to reach key populations. Assessing the efficiency of testing approaches requires a detailed understanding of their delivery and target populations. Different approaches may be cost-effective for different populations. To ensure hepatitis testing programs reach their intended populations and identify undiagnosed positive individuals, continuous monitoring and evaluation are required. The impact of testing approaches on uptake, positivity rates, costs, and changes in hepatitis B or C prevalence in different population groups must be regularly evaluated, and programs must be adjusted accordingly. Other activities include revising national targets and testing approaches to better reach undiagnosed individuals, developing a national consensus plan for expanding and refocusing hepatitis testing in line with treatment plans, and evaluating implemented programs through routine monitoring, program-specific evaluations, surveillance, and population-based surveys. Testing services require their own monitoring and evaluation framework. In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) published a monitoring and evaluation framework for hepatitis B and C, proposing ten core indicators, including the proportion of individuals living with HBV or HCV infection who are diagnosed.
